claim: Megakaryocytes (MKs) continuously produce platelets to support hemostasis.
source: Megakaryocytes (MKs) continuously produce platelets to support hemostasis and form a niche for hematopoietic stem cell maintenance in the bone marrow.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section (Deutsch and Tomer, 2006).

claim: Megakaryocytes form a niche for hematopoietic stem cell maintenance in the bone marrow.
source: Megakaryocytes (MKs) continuously produce platelets to support hemostasis and form a niche for hematopoietic stem cell maintenance in the bone marrow.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction (Bruns et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014).

claim: Using single-cell sequencing, a CXCR4 highly expressed MK subpopulation was identified.
source: Using single-cell sequencing, we identified a CXCR4 highly expressed MK subpopulation, which exhibited both MK-specific and immune characteristics.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by scRNA-seq data presented in Figure 1.

claim: CXCR4high MKs exhibited both MK-specific and immune characteristics.
source: Using single-cell sequencing, we identified a CXCR4 highly expressed MK subpopulation, which exhibited both MK-specific and immune characteristics.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: CXCR4high MKs interacted with myeloid cells to promote their migration.
source: CXCR4high MKs interacted with myeloid cells to promote their migration and stimulate the bacterial phagocytosis of macrophages and neutrophils by producing TNFα and IL-6.
evidence: This is supported by transwell migration assays shown in Figure 2D and spatial distribution analysis in Figure 2A-C.

claim: CXCR4high MKs stimulate the bacterial phagocytosis of macrophages and neutrophils by producing TNFα and IL-6.
source: CXCR4high MKs interacted with myeloid cells to promote their migration and stimulate the bacterial phagocytosis of macrophages and neutrophils by producing TNFα and IL-6.
evidence: This is supported by phagocytosis assays (Figure 2E-H) and cytokine blocking experiments (Figure 2K-N).

claim: CXCR4high MKs were capable of phagocytosis.
source: CXCR4high MKs were also capable of phagocytosis, processing, and presenting antigens to activate T cells.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial phagocytosis assays shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CXCR4high MKs were capable of processing and presenting antigens to activate T cells.
source: CXCR4high MKs were also capable of phagocytosis, processing, and presenting antigens to activate T cells.
evidence: This is supported by antigen presentation assays (Figure 3G-H) and T cell activation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: CXCR4high MKs egressed circulation and infiltrated into the spleen, liver, and lung upon bacterial infection.
source: Furthermore, CXCR4high MKs also egressed circulation and infiltrated into the spleen, liver, and lung upon bacterial infection.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4G, I, K) and immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 4N-O).

claim: Ablation of MKs suppressed the innate immune response under Listeria monocytogenes challenge.
source: Ablation of MKs suppressed the innate immune response and T cell activation to impair the anti-bacterial effects in mice under the Listeria monocytogenes challenge.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial burden measurements (Figure 3C) and myeloid cell quantification (Figure 3D-E) in MK-ablated mice.

claim: Ablation of MKs suppressed T cell activation under Listeria monocytogenes challenge.
source: Ablation of MKs suppressed the innate immune response and T cell activation to impair the anti-bacterial effects in mice under the Listeria monocytogenes challenge.
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays shown in Figure 3J.

claim: CXCR4high MKs were generated from infection-induced emergency megakaryopoiesis in response to bacterial infection.
source: Using hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell lineage-tracing mouse lines, we show that CXCR4high MKs were generated from infection-induced emergency megakaryopoiesis in response to bacterial infection.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments using SclCreER; Rosa26fs-tdTomato mice shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: MK progenitors undergo multiple rounds of endomitosis during maturation to achieve polyploidy.
source: MK progenitors undergo multiple rounds of endomitosis during maturation to achieve polyploidy (Chang et al., 2007; Deutsch and Tomer, 2013; Machlus and Italiano, 2013; Nagata et al., 1997; Patel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: MKs and their progenitors migrate between distinct microenvironments and organs for their proliferation, maturation, and biological functions.
source: MKs and their progenitors migrate between distinct microenvironments and organs for their proliferation, maturation, and biological functions (Avecilla et al., 2004; Fuentes et al., 2010; Lefrançais et al., 2017; Pal et al., 2020; Tamura et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mature MKs interact with HSCs and constitute a unique niche to preserve HSC quiescence in the bone marrow.
source: Mature MKs interact with HSCs and constitute a unique niche to preserve HSC quiescence in the bone marrow (Bruns et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MKs interact with osteoblasts to influence the attraction and retention of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: MKs also interact with other niche cells, such as osteoblasts (Dominici et al., 2009; Olson et al., 2013), non-myelinating Schwann cells (Jiang et al., 2018; Yamazaki et al., 2011), and blood vessels (Avecilla et al., 2004; Saçma et al., 2019) to further influence the attraction and retention of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells during homeostasis and stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MKs interact with non-myelinating Schwann cells to influence the attraction and retention of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: MKs also interact with other niche cells, such as osteoblasts (Dominici et al., 2009; Olson et al., 2013), non-myelinating Schwann cells (Jiang et al., 2018; Yamazaki et al., 2011), and blood vessels (Avecilla et al., 2004; Saçma et al., 2019) to further influence the attraction and retention of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells during homeostasis and stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MKs interact with blood vessels to influence the attraction and retention of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: MKs also interact with other niche cells, such as osteoblasts (Dominici et al., 2009; Olson et al., 2013), non-myelinating Schwann cells (Jiang et al., 2018; Yamazaki et al., 2011), and blood vessels (Avecilla et al., 2004; Saçma et al., 2019) to further influence the attraction and retention of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells during homeostasis and stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MK-biased hematopoietic stem cells induce emergency megakaryopoiesis to actively generate MKs upon acute inflammation.
source: MK-biased hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) induce emergency megakaryopoiesis to actively generate MKs upon acute inflammation, which can efficiently replenish the platelet loss during inflammatory insult (Haas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MKs express multiple immune receptors, such as IgG Fc receptors and toll-like receptors.
source: MKs express multiple immune receptors, such as IgG Fc receptors and toll-like receptors (TLRs), enabling them to sense inflammation directly (Cunin and Nigrovic, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mature MKs express major histocompatibility complex (MHC) to activate antigen-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: Mature MKs also express major histocompatibility complex (MHC) to activate antigen-specific CD8+ T cells and enhance CD4+ T cells and Th17 cell responses through stimulating antigen processing (Finkielsztein et al., 2015; Pariser et al., 2021; Zufferey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MKs produce IL-1α and IL-1β to promote arthritis susceptibility in mice resistant to arthritis.
source: For example, MKs produce IL-1α and IL-1β to promote arthritis susceptibility in mice resistant to arthritis (Cunin et al., 2017) and produce CXCL1 and CXCL2 to promote neutrophil efflux from the bone marrow (Köhler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MKs produce CXCL1 and CXCL2 to promote neutrophil efflux from the bone marrow.
source: For example, MKs produce IL-1α and IL-1β to promote arthritis susceptibility in mice resistant to arthritis (Cunin et al., 2017) and produce CXCL1 and CXCL2 to promote neutrophil efflux from the bone marrow (Köhler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Lung MKs contribute to thrombosis.
source: Lung MKs contribute to thrombosis (Lefrançais et al., 2017) and, more interestingly, participate in immune responses (Pariser et al., 2021), although the relationship between lung MKs and bone marrow circulating MKs (Nishimura et al., 2015) remains unexplored.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Lung MKs participate in immune responses.
source: Lung MKs contribute to thrombosis (Lefrançais et al., 2017) and, more interestingly, participate in immune responses (Pariser et al., 2021), although the relationship between lung MKs and bone marrow circulating MKs (Nishimura et al., 2015) remains unexplored.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MKs are heterogeneous and contain subpopulations that express multiple immune genes and are involved in inflammation response.
source: Furthermore, the recent single-cell atlas shows that MKs are heterogeneous and contain subpopulations that express multiple immune genes and are involved in inflammation response (Liu et al., 2021; Pariser et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2021; Yeung et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The scRNA-seq successfully detected 5368 high-quality cells.
source: Our scRNA-seq successfully detected 5368 high-quality cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), in which one MK cluster (1712 cells) and six immune cell clusters (3656 cells) were annotated according to their gene profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-G) and the alignment with published scRNA-seq data (Almanzar et al., 2020; Hamey et al., 2021; Pariser et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2020; Yeung et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: One MK cluster (1712 cells) and six immune cell clusters (3656 cells) were annotated.
source: Our scRNA-seq successfully detected 5368 high-quality cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), in which one MK cluster (1712 cells) and six immune cell clusters (3656 cells) were annotated according to their gene profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-G) and the alignment with published scRNA-seq data (Almanzar et al., 2020; Hamey et al., 2021; Pariser et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2020; Yeung et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1712 MKs were re-clustered into five subpopulations, termed MK1 to MK5.
source: Therefore, we re-clustered the transcriptionally enriched 1712 MKs into five subpopulations, termed MK1 to MK5 (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), which were further confirmed by the integrated scRNA-seq analysis platform to rule out the potential immune cell contamination (Pariser et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2020; Yeung et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: MK1 and MK2 highly expressed nuclear division, DNA replication and repair genes for endomitosis.
source: Enriched signature genes by Gene Ontology exhibited that MK1 and MK2 highly expressed nuclear division, DNA replication and repair genes for endomitosis (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: MK3 enriched blood coagulation and thrombosis genes for platelet generation.
source: MK3 enriched blood coagulation and thrombosis genes for platelet generation (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: MK5 enriched cell migration and immune response genes.
source: MK5 enriched cell migration and immune response genes (Figure 1C,D; Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-E), cytokine, chemokine (Figure 1E,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 4F), and genes involved in immune cell interaction (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: MK5 highly expressed Cxcr4 than other MK subpopulations.
source: We also noticed that MK5 highly expressed Cxcr4 than other MK subpopulations (Figure 1H,I), although most MKs express CXCR4 (Hamada et al., 1998; Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: CXCR4high MKs expressed MK markers.
source: To confirm this, we found that CXCR4high MKs expressed MK markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B), were mainly polyploid cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C), and had platelet generation ability (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D), although they have relatively low polyploidy (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E) and smaller cell size (Figure 1—figure supplement 6F-H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6B.

claim: CXCR4high MKs were mainly polyploid cells.
source: To confirm this, we found that CXCR4high MKs expressed MK markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B), were mainly polyploid cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C), and had platelet generation ability (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D), although they have relatively low polyploidy (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E) and smaller cell size (Figure 1—figure supplement 6F-H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6C.

claim: CXCR4high MKs had platelet generation ability.
source: To confirm this, we found that CXCR4high MKs expressed MK markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B), were mainly polyploid cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C), and had platelet generation ability (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D), although they have relatively low polyploidy (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E) and smaller cell size (Figure 1—figure supplement 6F-H).
evidence: This is supported by proplatelet formation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6D.

claim: CXCR4high MKs have relatively low polyploidy compared to CXCR4low MKs.
source: To confirm this, we found that CXCR4high MKs expressed MK markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B), were mainly polyploid cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C), and had platelet generation ability (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D), although they have relatively low polyploidy (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E) and smaller cell size (Figure 1—figure supplement 6F-H).
evidence: This is supported by polyploidy distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6E.

claim: CXCR4high MKs have smaller cell size compared to CXCR4low MKs.
source: To confirm this, we found that CXCR4high MKs expressed MK markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B), were mainly polyploid cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C), and had platelet generation ability (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D), although they have relatively low polyploidy (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E) and smaller cell size (Figure 1—figure supplement 6F-H).
evidence: This is supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6F-H.

claim: CXCR4high MKs generated platelets in lower efficiencies compared to CXCR4low MKs.
source: CXCR4high MKs generated platelets in lower efficiencies compared to CXCR4low MKs (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D), suggesting CXCR4high MKs might be specialized for immune functions.
evidence: This is supported by proplatelet formation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6D.

claim: CXCR4high MKs might be specialized for immune functions.
source: CXCR4high MKs generated platelets in lower efficiencies compared to CXCR4low MKs (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D), suggesting CXCR4high MKs might be specialized for immune functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CXCR4high MKs have lower platelet generation efficiency but high immune gene expression.

claim: CXCR4high MKs were more dramatically associated with myeloid cells in the bone marrow of mice 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that CXCR4high MKs were more dramatically associated with myeloid cells in the bone marrow of mice 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection, which was a significant increase than the association between myeloid cells and CXCR4low MKs or the association between randomly placed myeloid cells and CXCR4high MKs (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The myeloid cell-CXCR4high MK association (mean distance 15.36 μm) was significantly closer than the myeloid cell-CXCR4low MKs association (mean distance 25.62 μm).
source: The myeloid cell-CXCR4high MK association (mean distance 15.36 μm) was significantly closer than the myeloid cell-CXCR4low MKs association (Figure 2C; mean distance 25.62 μm, p=7.0 × 10–4 by KS test), and the association between randomly placed myeloid cells and CXCR4high MKs [35.37 μm, p (μ<15.36)=1.8 × 10–10] in the bone marrow of mice 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
evidence: This is supported by distance measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CXCR4high MKs, but not CXCR4low MKs, effectively promoted myeloid cell mobilization in transwell assays.
source: To explore how CXCR4high MKs regulate myeloid cells, we interestingly found that CXCR4high MKs, but not CXCR4low MKs, effectively promoted myeloid cell mobilization in our transwell assays (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by transwell migration assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CXCR4high MKs, but not CXCR4low MKs, efficiently enhanced the bacterial phagocytosis of neutrophils and macrophages.
source: We found that CXCR4high MKs, but not CXCR4low MKs, efficiently enhanced the bacterial phagocytosis of neutrophils and macrophages (Figure 2E–H; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by phagocytosis assays shown in Figure 2E-H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: The high expression of Cxcr4 was positively correlated with immune cell-stimulating cytokines, such as Ccl6, Tnf, and Il6 in MKs.
source: Our scRNA-seq also exhibited that the high expression of Cxcr4 was positively correlated with immune cell-stimulating cytokines, such as Ccl6, Tnf, and Il6 (Li et al., 2018; Rothe et al., 1993; Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018) in MKs (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: CXCR4high MKs had higher TNFα and IL-6 protein levels than CXCR4low MKs.
source: In line with this, CXCR4high MKs had higher TNFα and IL-6 protein levels than CXCR4low MKs (Figure 2J; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: The TNFα and IL-6 levels in CXCR4high MKs were comparable to macrophages from mice 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: The TNFα and IL-6 levels in CXCR4high MKs were comparable to macrophages from mice 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), which are known as the primary cellular source of TNFα and IL-6 upon infection (Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Anti-TNFα and anti-IL-6 blocking antibodies compromised the role of CXCR4high MKs in stimulating bacterial phagocytosis of neutrophils and macrophages.
source: Indeed, anti-TNFα and anti-IL-6 blocking antibodies compromised the role of CXCR4high MKs in stimulating bacterial phagocytosis of neutrophils and macrophages (Figure 2K–N).
evidence: This is supported by phagocytosis assays with blocking antibodies shown in Figure 2K-N.

claim: MK ablation increased the number of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and myelopoiesis in the bone marrow upon infection.
source: MK ablation increased the number of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and myelopoiesis in the bone marrow upon infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: MK ablation dramatically increased the bacterial burdens in the liver and spleen 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Notably, MK ablation dramatically increased the bacterial burdens in the liver and spleen 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial burden measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MK ablation reduced the number of myeloid cells, including monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells (DCs), and neutrophils, in the liver and spleen.
source: We also found that MK ablation reduced the number of myeloid cells, including monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells (DCs), and neutrophils, in the liver and spleen (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F), suggesting the role of MKs in promoting myeloid cells against pathogens.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: CXCR4high MKs were able to phagocytose bacteria.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that CXCR4high MKs were able to phagocytose bacteria and presented the ovalbumin (OVA) antigens on their surface via MHC-I (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by phagocytosis assays shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CXCR4high MKs presented the ovalbumin (OVA) antigens on their surface via MHC-I.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that CXCR4high MKs were able to phagocytose bacteria and presented the ovalbumin (OVA) antigens on their surface via MHC-I (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by MHC-I-OVA staining shown in Figure 3G.

claim: OVA antigens presented by CXCR4high MKs activated OT-I CD8+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, OVA antigens presented by CXCR4high MKs activated OT-I CD8+ T cells (Figure 3H) and B3Z T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), a T cell hybridoma which expresses TCR that specifically recognizes OVA (Karttunen et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: OVA antigens presented by CXCR4high MKs activated B3Z T cells.
source: Furthermore, OVA antigens presented by CXCR4high MKs activated OT-I CD8+ T cells (Figure 3H) and B3Z T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), a T cell hybridoma which expresses TCR that specifically recognizes OVA (Karttunen et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by T cell activation assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: MK ablation dramatically reduced the number of CD4+ IFNγ+ Th1, CD4+ IL4+ Th2, and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
source: Notably, MK ablation dramatically reduced the number of CD4+ IFNγ+ Th1, CD4+ IL4+ Th2, and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes but did not impact the total number of CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The infusion with CXCR4high MKs, but not CXCR4low MKs, partially rescued the bacterial clearance defect in MK ablation mice.
source: Notably, we found that the infusion with CXCR4high MKs, but not CXCR4low MKs, partially rescued the bacterial clearance defect in MK ablation mice (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial burden measurements shown in Figure 3L.

claim: ~80% of MKs directly contacted blood vessels 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: In line with this, our spatial distribution analysis showed that ~80% of MKs directly contacted blood vessels 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection, which was much higher than in control mice (~40%) (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: More CXCR4high MKs, with small cell sizes, were tightly associated with blood vessels and trapped in the sinusoid than CXCR4low MKs 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Furthermore, more CXCR4high MKs, with small cell sizes (Figure 1—figure supplement 6F-H), were tightly associated with blood vessels and trapped in the sinusoid than CXCR4low MKs 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution analysis and immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: L. monocytogenes infection did not influence the association between MKs and HSCs.
source: However, L. monocytogenes infection did not influence the association between MKs and HSCs (Figure 4A,E), albeit the critical role of perivascular MKs in maintaining HSC quiescence (Bruns et al., 2014; Itkin et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2014) and the dramatic HSC activation upon infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 4A and 4E.

claim: Small tdTomato+ MKs rapidly migrated into sinusoids without rupture or platelet release upon infection.
source: Using Pf4Cre; Rosa26fs-tdTomato mice and ex vivo live imaging approach, we observed that small tdTomato+ MKs rapidly migrated into sinusoids without rupture or platelet release upon infection (Figure 4F, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: MKs with large sizes showed much slower migration than small MKs.
source: In contrast, MKs with large sizes showed much slower migration (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4—video 1.

claim: CXCR4high MKs were decreased in the bone marrow 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Additionally, CXCR4high MKs were decreased in the bone marrow 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection but with a similar proliferation and apoptosis rate compared to CXCR4low MKs (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-F), indicating CXCR4high MKs might migrate out of bone marrow.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The frequency of MK5, which enriched CXCR4high MKs, decreased in bone marrow after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Consistent with this, the frequency of MK5, which enriched CXCR4high MKs, decreased in bone marrow after L. monocytogenes infection in our single-cell atlas (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: L. monocytogenes infection decreased the expression of CXCL12 in bone marrow but increased CXCL12 expression in the lung, liver, and spleen.
source: Furthermore, we found that L. monocytogenes infection decreased the expression of CXCL12, the ligand of CXCR4 (Sugiyama et al., 2006), in bone marrow but increased CXCL12 expression in the lung, liver, and spleen (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the distinguished CXCL12 levels between tissues might drive the migration of CXCR4high MKs between tissues.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: CXCR4high MKs were increased in the peripheral blood and organs, including the liver, spleen, and lung 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: In line with this, CXCR4high MKs were increased in the peripheral blood and organs, including the liver, spleen, and lung 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection without an alternation of cell cycle and apoptosis, whereas CXCR4low MKs did not differ except for a slight increase in the liver (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-C.

claim: Inflammatory stresses, such as IFNγ and Lipopolysaccharides (LPS), or L. monocytogenes treatment did not increase CXCR4 expression in CXCR4low MKs.
source: Moreover, inflammatory stresses, such as IFNγ and Lipopolysaccharides (LPS), or L. monocytogenes treatment did not increase CXCR4 expression in CXCR4low MKs (Figure 4H; Figure 4—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 4D.

claim: mGFP expressing MKs or Tomato expressing CXCR4high MKs were increased in the liver and spleen 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: mGFP expressing MKs or Tomato expressing CXCR4high MKs were increased in the liver and spleen 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 4E-H), whereas Tomato expressing CXCR4low MKs did not change (Figure 4—figure supplement 4I).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 4E-H.

claim: Engrafted mTomato+ CXCR4high MKs more efficiently infiltrated into the liver (92.1%) and spleen (92.5%).
source: We found that 2 days after mTomato+ cell perfusion, engrafted mTomato+ CXCR4high MKs more efficiently infiltrated into the liver (92.1%) and spleen (92.5%); by contrast, most mTomato+ CXCR4low MKs (66.7%) migrated to the bone marrow (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: MK5, MK4, and MK3 showed similar gene profiles with lung MKs.
source: As the lung is an important site for platelet generation (Lefrançais et al., 2017), we aligned our MK sc-RNAseq data with lung MKs (Pariser et al., 2021; Yeung et al., 2020), and found that MK5, MK4, and MK3 showed similar gene profiles with lung MKs (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic similarity analysis shown in Figure 4L.

claim: MK5 enriched more inflammatory pathway genes, antigen processing, and presentation pathway after L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Moreover, MK5 enriched more inflammatory pathway genes, antigen processing, and presentation pathway after L. monocytogenes infection, which enabled MK5 to achieve a more similar transcriptional profile as the lung MKs than normal MK5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by gene set variation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Engrafted Tomato+ MKs more efficiently infiltrated the lungs in the infected recipients as extravascular MKs than in the control recipients.
source: Interestingly, we found that engrafted Tomato+ MKs (from Pf4Cre; Rosa26fs-tdTomato mice) more efficiently infiltrated the lungs in the infected recipients as extravascular MKs than in the control recipients (Figure 4M–O and Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4M-O and Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: MKs were ruptured in the bone marrow 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection to recover the reduced platelets post-L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Consistently, we observed that MKs were ruptured in the bone marrow 3 days after L. monocytogenes infection to recover the reduced platelets post-L. monocytogenes infection (Couldwell and Machlus, 2019; Nishimura et al., 2015; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and platelet counts shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: CXCR4high MKs were increased at 18 hr after L. monocytogenes infection and substantially declined at 72 hr in bone marrow.
source: However, CXCR4high MKs were increased at 18 hr after L. monocytogenes infection and substantially declined at 72 hr in bone marrow, whereas CXCR4low MKs remained unchanged upon infection (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Tomato+ HSPCs derived Tomato+ CXCR4high MKs rapidly increased in the bone marrow 18 hours after tamoxifen recombining Tomato in HSPCs and L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Eighteen hours after tamoxifen recombining Tomato in HSPCs and L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 5E), we observed that Tomato+ HSPCs derived Tomato+ CXCR4high MKs rapidly increased in the bone marrow, similar to the platelet-generating MKs (tdTomato+ CXCR4low MKs) (Figure 5F), without a noticeable rise of hematopoietic progenitors (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: MKs prevent the spread of dengue virus infection by enhancing the type 1 interferons pathway in murine and clinical biospecimens.
source: Accordingly, MKs prevent the spread of dengue virus infection by enhancing the type 1 interferons pathway in murine and clinical biospecimens (Campbell et al., 2019) and contribute to cytokine storms in severe COVID-19 patients (Bernardes et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2021; Stephenson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MKs contribute to cytokine storms in severe COVID-19 patients.
source: Accordingly, MKs prevent the spread of dengue virus infection by enhancing the type 1 interferons pathway in murine and clinical biospecimens (Campbell et al., 2019) and contribute to cytokine storms in severe COVID-19 patients (Bernardes et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2021; Stephenson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MK ablation increased HSPCS and myeloid granulocyte/macrophage progenitor (GMP) in bone marrow under bacterial infection.
source: We observed that MK ablation increased HSPCS and myeloid granulocyte/macrophage progenitor (GMP) in bone marrow under bacterial infection, which is consistent with 5-FU stress (Hérault et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Normal HSC to MK development takes 11–12 days in humans and 4 days in mice.
source: Normal HSC to MK development takes 11–12 days in humans and 4 days in mice; However, emergency megakaryopoiesis takes less than a day to generate MKs upon inflammation stress (Couldwell and Machlus, 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2021; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Emergency megakaryopoiesis takes less than a day to generate MKs upon inflammation stress.
source: Normal HSC to MK development takes 11–12 days in humans and 4 days in mice; However, emergency megakaryopoiesis takes less than a day to generate MKs upon inflammation stress (Couldwell and Machlus, 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2021; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Inflammation signals could not upregulate CXCR4 in CXCR4low MKs in vitro.
source: Previously, researchers believed that emergency megakaryopoiesis mainly contributes to the replenishment of damaged platelets upon acute inflammation (Haas et al., 2015). We found that inflammation signals could not upregulate CXCR4 in CXCR4low MKs in vitro, although we cannot entirely exclude the plasticity of MKs in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The lung is a reservoir of MKs for platelet production.
source: A recent report showed that the lung is a reservoir of MKs for platelet production (Lefrançais et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Lung MKs share a similar transcriptional profile with lung DCs and participate in pathogen infection.
source: Other works also indicate that lung MKs share a similar transcriptional profile with lung DCs and participate in pathogen infection (Boilard and Machlus, 2021; Pariser et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neonatal lung MKs lack the immune molecules in adult lung MKs.
source: Neonatal lung MKs lack the immune molecules in adult lung MKs (Pariser et al., 2021), which indicates that lung MKs might have distinct developmental origins.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MKs are observed to egress and migrate to the pulmonary capillary under stresses.
source: Similarly, MKs are observed to egress and migrate to the pulmonary capillary under stresses (Davis et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Lung MKs might migrate from bone marrow upon infection challenges.
source: Our works suggested lung MKs might migrate from bone marrow upon infection challenges, although more detailed investigations are warranted in future studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing CXCR4high MKs infiltrating the lung upon infection (Figure 4M-O).
